## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and the starting architecture scores 0.000 on both seeds. Under the default recipe the budget is only about 32 PPO updates of 4096 steps, so the starting architecture's failure may come from too little training as much as from the architecture. Using fewer PPO epochs buys more fresh samples within the same compute. Smaller minibatches give more gradient steps. A slightly higher gamma should help credit the +1 exact-build bonus and teach DONE. On the architecture side, the starting head pools features over a brick's footprint only after mixing all layers into one set of column features. Placement correctness depends on the landing layer, which is the highest filled layer under the footprint. So pooling over the footprint separately for each layer (any/all occupied, any/all missing at each z) should make it easier to tell whether the landing cells are all missing and whether the brick seals needed cells below it. This round separates the recipe effect (C1) from the architecture effect (C2), and C3 tests a recipe with even more samples.

### Round 2
All three trials scored exactly 0, on dev and on training (last 10%). That held across 1.7–3x more samples, 1–4 PPO epochs and a per-layer pooling head. Because nothing has worked yet, the seed-noise figure cannot tell these trials apart. More samples alone did not help, so I don't think the recipe is the main bottleneck. The networks probably can't learn the per-step rule of the task quickly enough. That rule: a brick lands at the highest build height under its footprint (L). The placement is correct only if every footprint cell at L is missing from the build and no missing cells lie below L, so nothing gets sealed. It must hold for every step of an episode. My next step: an explicitly per-layer scorer. For each layer and each brick type, it scores the placement from min/max pools of learned per-layer cell embeddings, then takes a soft maximum over layers. The three candidates test this structure, a recipe change, and a learned scan across layers.

### Round 3
Six trials all scored 0 on dev, and also 0 on training success: no stochastic rollout ever produced an exact build. That held across sample counts (135k to 389k), PPO epochs (1 to 3) and three head designs. Seed noise can't explain six zeros out of six. Recipe tweaks alone don't seem to help. Every network so far shares one assumption: the action anchor is the top-left corner, so footprint pooling is aligned right and down. The trunks were also shallow, with a 5x5 receptive field. If this world's anchor convention, axis order or footprint orientation differs from the description, those heads are misaligned, and the network would have to learn to correct for that on top of everything else. This round drops that assumption. Two heads are tested: a convolutional head (a 3x3 per-type head added to a learned map from the whole board to every action), and a cell transformer with learned positions that can learn any mapping from cell to action. A recipe variant of the first tests a longer horizon and more sample reuse.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and in training, across three head designs (footprint pooling, per-layer scoring, dense conv and attention) and recipes from 1 to 4 epochs and 86k to 389k steps. Seed noise cannot explain that many identical zeros, so something blocks learning that none of these changes touched. One likely cause is collapse onto DONE. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target and earn negative reward, while DONE earns 0. DONE is a single logit shared by every state, so it learns fast. Pushing all placement logits down together has the same effect as pushing DONE up. Once DONE dominates, episodes last one step, placements are never explored, and success stays at 0. For the last round I make DONE's odds relative to the average placement logit, so a shared shift in placement logits cannot raise DONE. I test this on two different networks and with a slower DONE plus higher entropy.
